perspective: Graph theorist: glyph tracing is the Route Inspection (Chinese Postman) problem on the skeleton's pixel adjacency graph, generalized to multigraphs with multiple connected components, with the twist that we are allowed (and required) to use multiple open trails rather than a single closed circuit. The right primitive is the T-join: a minimum-weight edge set whose addition makes the graph Eulerian on a chosen number of trails. Stroke choreography (which trail starts where, in which direction) is a secondary lift on top of an edge-cover decomposition that is already optimal.
algorithm_overview: Treat the cleaned skeleton as an undirected multigraph G = (V, E) with integer edge weights = arc length in pixels. A "stroke" is a trail (walk with no repeated edges); a stroke decomposition is a partition of E into trails T_1, ..., T_N. The classical theorem (Euler / Listing): a connected multigraph with 2k odd-degree vertices decomposes into exactly max(k,1) edge-disjoint trails, and into a single closed trail iff k = 0. Retracing is unavoidable only if we insist on fewer trails than k; then we must duplicate edges to lower the odd-degree count, and the optimal duplication is the minimum-weight T-join on the odd-degree set (the Chinese Postman LP). So the algorithm is: (1) per connected component, decide the desired number of trails N_C (driven by a "handwriting plausibility" budget); (2) reduce parity by adding the minimum-weight T-join over the odd vertices to bring odd-count to 2*N_C; (3) for each component run Hierholzer on the now-Eulerian (multi)graph to extract trails; (4) split into N_C trails by cutting Hierholzer's single circuit at the chosen odd vertices, or at "natural" hinge vertices if none; (5) order and orient trails by a writing-economy objective (top-to-bottom, left-to-right starts, minimize pen-up distance between consecutive trails). Steps 1-4 are pure graph theory and have no per-letter heuristics. Step 5 is the only place choreography enters, and it is a small TSP over endpoints.

core_steps.name: Preprocess: build cleaned multigraph with arc-length weights
core_steps.rationale: Hierholzer and T-join both want a multigraph where each edge is a single arc with a stored polyline path and a real-valued length. We already have skeleton_to_graph + merge_nearby_junctions + collapse_parallel_edges producing exactly this. Crucially we keep self-loops (bowl of 'a', the 'o') — Euler theory handles loops natively: a self-loop contributes 2 to the degree of its endpoint, so it does not change parity.
core_steps.pseudocode:
G_pix = build_skel_pixel_graph(skel)              # 8-conn pixel graph, for shortest paths only
G = skeleton_to_graph(skel)                         # multigraph: nodes = endpoints + junctions
G = merge_nearby_junctions(G, max_dist=22)          # collapse X-crossing clusters
G = collapse_parallel_edges(G, dist_map)            # collapse medial-axis splits, KEEP enclosed bowls
for (u,v,k) in G.edges:
    G[u][v][k]['len'] = polyline_length(G[u][v][k]['path'])
components = list(nx.connected_components(G))
core_steps.edge_cases: (1) An isolated vertex (a tittle on 'i' after pruning collapses to a single pixel) is its own component with 0 edges — emit a 'dot' stroke of length 0 and skip Hierholzer. (2) A component whose entire skeleton is a single self-loop (the 'o') has one vertex of degree 2 and zero odd vertices — Hierholzer produces a closed circuit; we cut it at the topmost point. (3) merge_nearby_junctions can produce a degree-1 self-loop pair if a short stub gets absorbed — drop zero-length edges before Hierholzer.

core_steps.name: Per-component odd-vertex enumeration and trail-count target
core_steps.rationale: Euler's theorem: a connected graph with O odd-degree vertices admits a single closed Eulerian circuit iff O = 0, a single open Eulerian trail iff O = 2, and decomposes into exactly O/2 edge-disjoint open trails in general (no retracing) — this is a classical result (Listing 1836; see Bondy and Murty Thm 4.5). So the cost-free minimum trail count is N_free = max(1, O/2). We pick the target N as N_free unless a handwriting prior wants to split further (e.g., split the closed 'o' into one open trail).
core_steps.pseudocode:
for C in components:
    G_C = G.subgraph(C).copy()
    odd = [v for v in G_C.nodes if G_C.degree(v) % 2 == 1]
    O = len(odd)
    N_free = max(1, O // 2)
    # Handwriting prior: open closed components by one cut, but never force
    # MORE retracing than Euler demands.
    if O == 0 and G_C.number_of_edges() > 0:
        N_target[C] = 1   # one closed trail; we will cut it post-hoc
    else:
        N_target[C] = N_free
core_steps.edge_cases: Degree parity is computed on the MULTIgraph (self-loops add 2, parallel edges each add 1). If collapse_parallel_edges left a true double edge (e.g., the spine of a very bold 'I' that didn't pass the area test), both edges count and the endpoints are even — Hierholzer will traverse both, which is the correct 'down then back up' double-stroke behavior.

core_steps.name: T-join parity repair (only when we want FEWER trails than O/2)
core_steps.rationale: If the desired N is below O/2 we must duplicate edges to make 2N vertices odd. The minimum total duplicated length is the minimum-weight T-join on the symmetric difference of 'currently odd' and 'desired-odd' sets. For Chinese Postman this is solved exactly by min-weight perfect matching on the complete graph over the odd vertices, with edge weight = shortest-path length in G. We do NOT need this step for Latin letters in the default policy (N = O/2), but it is the principled lever for 'I want to write A in 2 strokes instead of 3.'
core_steps.edge_cases: (a) min_weight_matching on |to_fix| vertices: requires |to_fix| even — guaranteed because every connected graph has an even number of odd-degree vertices (handshake lemma). (b) When N = O/2 (the default), want_odd_set = cur_odd and to_fix is empty — no duplication. (c) Self-loops in the duplication path are fine (they cost 2L but contribute 0 to parity, so the matcher will never pick them unless forced).

core_steps.name: Hierholzer per component: extract Eulerian trail(s)
core_steps.rationale: Once parity is right, Hierholzer's algorithm (1873) extracts an Eulerian trail in O(|E|). For a connected multigraph with 2k odd vertices and k ≥ 1, run Hierholzer starting from any odd vertex and it returns one trail covering all edges if k = 1; for k > 1, we pair up odd vertices, virtually add k-1 'ghost' edges between paired odd vertices to make the graph have exactly 2 odd vertices, run Hierholzer once, then split the result at ghost edges. Pairing choice = handwriting choreography, deferred to step 5.
core_steps.pseudocode:
def decompose_component(G_C):
    odd = sorted(v for v in G_C.nodes if G_C.degree(v) % 2 == 1)
    if len(odd) == 0:
        # Closed component (e.g., 'o'). Pick a topmost vertex as cut point.
        start = min(G_C.nodes, key=lambda v: (v[0], v[1]))
        circuit = hierholzer_circuit(G_C, start)   # list of edges
        return [circuit]                            # caller may cut later
    pairs = pair_odd_vertices(odd, G_C)             # handwriting-aware, step 5
    ghost = []
    G_aug = G_C.copy()
    for (u, v) in pairs[1:]:                        # leave first pair as trail endpoints
        kkey = G_aug.add_edge(u, v, len=0.0, path=[u, v], ghost=True)
        ghost.append((u, v, kkey))
    start, end = pairs[0]
    trail = hierholzer_trail(G_aug, start, end)     # list of (u,v,k) edges
    # Cut at ghost edges to recover len(pairs) separate trails
    sub_trails, cur = [], []
    for (u, v, k) in trail:
        if G_aug[u][v][k].get('ghost'):
            sub_trails.append(cur); cur = []
        else:
            cur.append((u, v, k))
    sub_trails.append(cur)
    return sub_trails
core_steps.edge_cases: (1) The ghost-edge trick requires the augmented graph to remain connected after ghost insertion — it always is (we only added edges). (2) hierholzer_trail must be the standard stack-based variant that handles multigraphs (track edge KEYS, not just (u,v) pairs); networkx's nx.eulerian_path works on MultiGraph and consumes edge keys via 'eulerian_circuit(..., keys=True)'. (3) For a single-self-loop component the trail is just the loop edge — works without special-casing.

core_steps.name: Odd-vertex pairing (handwriting prior, the only 'taste' step)
core_steps.rationale: When O = 2k with k > 1, there are (2k)! / (2^k k!) ways to pair odd vertices into k trails. Each pairing is a valid edge-disjoint trail decomposition. We minimize a writing-cost objective: prefer pairings whose trails (a) start high and left, (b) move predominantly downward and rightward, (c) avoid sharp reversals at junctions. This is a small assignment problem (k ≤ 4 for almost all Latin letters), solvable by brute force or Hungarian.
core_steps.pseudocode:
def pair_odd_vertices(odd, G_C):
    best = None; best_cost = +inf
    for matching in all_perfect_matchings(odd):           # (2k)!/(2^k k!) of them
        cost = 0.0
        for (u, v) in matching:
            # heuristic but well-defined: a trail from upper-left to lower-right is cheap
            cost += alpha * (writing_order_penalty(u, v))
            cost += beta  * (junction_reversal_penalty(u, v, G_C))
        if cost < best_cost:
            best_cost = cost; best = matching
    # Sort so the 'first' pair is the one with the highest, leftmost start —
    # that becomes the start/end of the master Hierholzer call.
    best.sort(key=lambda p: (min(p[0][0], p[1][0]), min(p[0][1], p[1][1])))
    return best

def writing_order_penalty(u, v):
    # Prefer u above v and u left of v; squared so big inversions hurt more.
    top, bot = (u, v) if u[0] < v[0] else (v, u)
    dy = bot[0] - top[0]; dx = bot[1] - top[1]
    return -(dy + 0.3 * dx)         # negative → reward downward+rightward trails
core_steps.edge_cases: (1) For k = 1 (one trail) there is exactly one matching; this code returns immediately. (2) When two odd vertices are at exactly the same y, x tiebreak chooses left-start. (3) The junction_reversal_penalty discourages a pairing that forces Hierholzer to enter and leave a junction along nearly-collinear edges with a sharp angle — that's the only place tangent geometry enters, and it is purely a tiebreaker.

core_steps.name: Component-level closed-loop cutting
core_steps.rationale: If a component had O = 0 (the letter 'o', the bowl-only component after a degree-2 'b' is processed in two pieces), Hierholzer returns a CIRCUIT, not a trail. Handwriting wants an open path. We cut it at the geometrically natural pen-down point: topmost, leftmost. This is a single rotation of the cyclic edge list — zero retracing introduced.
core_steps.pseudocode:
def open_closed_circuit(circuit, G_C):
    # circuit is a cyclic list of (u,v,k). Find the index whose tail vertex u
    # has the smallest (y, x).
    verts = [e[0] for e in circuit]
    i_cut = min(range(len(circuit)), key=lambda i: (verts[i][0], verts[i][1]))
    return circuit[i_cut:] + circuit[:i_cut]
core_steps.edge_cases: (1) A degenerate single-edge self-loop circuit has length 1 and the rotation is a no-op — still correct. (2) If the topmost point lies in the MIDDLE of an edge polyline (not at a graph vertex), we either accept a slightly-off cut at the nearest vertex or subdivide the edge by inserting a synthetic degree-2 node at the topmost pixel and re-run from step 4. The synthetic-node variant is preferable for the visually-symmetric 'o'.

core_steps.name: Inter-trail ordering (a tiny TSP)
core_steps.rationale: Step 4 returns a set of trails per component, and step 1 gave us multiple components. Final emission order is a TSP over trail endpoints with a pen-down cost. With at most ~6 trails per letter this is solved by exact DP in microseconds. Tie-break favors top-to-bottom, left-to-right for the start of each trail.
core_steps.pseudocode:
def order_trails(all_trails):
    # each trail has (start_xy, end_xy, can_reverse=True)
    n = len(all_trails)
    # Held–Karp DP, with each trail visited in either orientation.
    # State: (subset of visited trails, last trail index, last orientation).
    # Cost between trails: pen-up Euclidean distance from previous end to next start,
    # plus a writing-order bias (penalty if next start is above previous end).
    return held_karp(all_trails, cost_fn=pen_up_plus_top_left_bias)
core_steps.edge_cases: (1) For a 1-component, 1-trail letter ('l'), this is a no-op. (2) For 'i' and 'j' we get two components (stem + dot). The TSP correctly orders stem-first-then-dot because the dot is small and far, and crossing back upward to the dot has a real pen-up cost matched against the writing-order bias — for 'i', humans draw stem then dot, and this comes out for free.

handles_letters.topology_class: single-loop (one closed cycle, one degree-2 vertex)
handles_letters.notes: After skeleton_to_graph the medial axis of 'o' is a single closed curve. There are no degree-1 or degree-≥3 vertices, so the graph has one vertex of degree 2 (or none, depending on how we encode a pure cycle — see edge case below). O = 0, so N_free = 1 closed trail. Hierholzer produces the full circuit; step 6 cuts it at the topmost point. Result: one trail tracing the entire 'o' counterclockwise (or clockwise, depending on which neighbor Hierholzer picks first — handwriting prior can flip orientation to match the convention). EDGE CASE: a pure cycle has no degree-1 or degree-≥3 vertices, so skeleton_to_graph as written produces NO graph nodes — must insert a synthetic degree-2 anchor at the topmost pixel before building the multigraph for closed components.

Two degree-1 endpoints (top, bottom), no junctions. O = 2 ⇒ N_free = 1. Hierholzer from the top endpoint traces the whole stem to the bottom. Pairing step is trivial (one pair). Writing-order penalty correctly chooses top as start. Zero retracing, single trail. This is the simplest non-trivial case and confirms the algorithm reproduces sane behavior without templates.

handles_letters.topology_class: tree-with-2-junctions (Y/Y shape: two top branches, crossbar, two legs)
handles_letters.notes: After junction merging, 'A' has 4 endpoints (2 leg tips + 2 crossbar-only-if-it-protrudes... actually after a clean medial axis: 2 leg tips + the apex) and 2 internal junctions where the crossbar meets each leg. Degrees: 2 leg-tip endpoints (deg 1) + 1 apex (deg 1 or 2 depending on font) + 2 junctions (deg 3 each). Odd count O = 4 (two leg tips + two junctions if apex is degree 2) or O = 5 (impossible by handshake — so O is 4 or 6). For O = 4: N_free = 2 trails with zero retrace. The natural human decomposition is 3 strokes (left leg down, right leg down, crossbar) which costs ONE duplicated edge (retrace half the crossbar) — that is the T-join repair telling us human writing is graph-suboptimal by 1 small edge. Default policy of N = N_free gives 2 strokes (one long zig-zag down-left-leg then up-and-over to crossbar then down-right-leg, plus crossbar as second trail) — visually unusual but topologically minimal. To force 3 strokes we set want_odd to include both junctions (each becomes a trail endpoint), pay the T-join cost of half a crossbar, and Hierholzer + ghost-edge splitting yields exactly the human decomposition.

handles_letters.topology_class: tree-with-2-junctions (W-shape: 4 endpoints, 2 internal junctions OR pure path)
handles_letters.notes: If the middle V of 'M' meets the outer legs at a SHARP angle, skeleton_to_graph sees a single zigzag path with 2 endpoints and 3 degree-2 turning points — O = 2, N_free = 1, one trail does it all (up-down-up-down). If the middle V meets the outer legs at FLAT internal junctions (3-way), then we have 2 leg-tip endpoints (deg 1), 1 middle-V apex (deg 1), and 2 junctions (deg 3) — O = 5 which is impossible, so really O = 4 or 6. For a clean rendering O = 2 and the algorithm gives the single-trail human stroke. EDGE: the order it picks (left-leg-up first vs left-leg-down first) is decided by writing_order_penalty preferring the LEFT-START, which matches handwriting convention.

Lowercase 'm' has 4 degree-1 endpoints (3 bottom feet + the top-left start of the first downstroke is shared with a foot in a true medial-axis skeleton — really 3 foot endpoints) and 2 deg-3 junctions at the tops of the second and third arches. Typical O = 4 or O = 2 depending on top topology. For typical sans: O = 4, N_free = 2. The natural human decomposition is 1 trail ('first downstroke, up-over-down, up-over-down'); this is one trail with TWO retraced segments (the upstrokes inside each arch). T-join repair targeting want_odd = {first-foot, last-foot} adds the two short retraces and yields the human one-stroke 'm'. This letter is the canonical example of human writing being graph-suboptimal: minimum-retrace = 2 trails, but humans choose 1 trail + small retrace.

handles_letters.topology_class: tree-with-1-junction (stem + bowl attached at one point)
handles_letters.notes: After merge_nearby_junctions the bowl attaches to the stem at one degree-3 junction. Endpoints: top of stem (deg 1), bottom of stem (deg 1, identical to bottom of bowl if bowl closes onto stem-bottom). If bowl meets stem at TWO points (top and bottom of bowl both touch stem), we have one junction or two; the graph has 2 endpoints (top of stem + ??) and a cycle. With a single-junction attachment, deg-3 junction has odd degree, stem-top is odd, so O = 2 and N_free = 1: Hierholzer from stem-top goes down stem to junction, around the bowl back to junction, and... we've used all edges. One trail. With two-junction (top-bowl and bottom-bowl meeting stem separately) we get O = 4 and N_free = 2, which gives the 'stem then bowl' two-stroke human decomposition for free.

Stem with two bowls attached. Endpoints: stem-top (deg 1), stem-bottom (deg 1). Junctions: middle of stem where the two bowls meet (deg 4 if both bowls share the middle node, else two deg-3 nodes). With deg-4 middle node: O = 2 (just stem ends), N_free = 1, Hierholzer does it all in one trail with both bowls traced consecutively. With two deg-3 middle nodes: O = 4, N_free = 2, giving the canonical 'stem first, then both bowls as a figure-8 second stroke' — close to human writing, which is usually 'stem then top bowl then bottom bowl' (3 strokes). T-join repair targeting want_odd = {stem-top, stem-bottom, top-bowl-cusp, bottom-bowl-cusp} forces 3 strokes by duplicating one small edge.

Crossbar crosses stem at one deg-4 junction (after merging). Endpoints: top-of-stem, bottom-of-stem, left-crossbar, right-crossbar — 4 endpoints, all deg 1 ⇒ O = 4, N_free = 2. Pairing step picks {top-stem, bottom-stem} and {left-crossbar, right-crossbar} as the lower-cost matching (writing_order_penalty rewards vertical pair + horizontal pair over diagonal pairs). Result: stem stroke (top to bottom) then crossbar (left to right). Exactly the human decomposition. Inter-trail TSP sequences them stem-first (higher start) then crossbar.

handles_letters.topology_class: tree-with-2-junctions (stem + V-arm joined at one junction)
handles_letters.notes: Stem (2 endpoints) + a V-shaped arm (2 endpoints) meeting the stem at one deg-4 junction (or one deg-3 + one deg-3 if the V's apex is on the stem). Deg-4 case: O = 4 ⇒ N_free = 2. Pairing picks {top-stem, bottom-stem} and {upper-arm-tip, lower-arm-tip}, giving the human 'stem then V-arm' two-stroke decomposition. If the V joins the stem at the same point as a kink (deg-3 + deg-3), O = 4 still, same result. The pairing-cost objective correctly prefers the vertical-with-vertical and diagonal-with-diagonal pairing over the mixed pairing.

Two connected components: stem (path graph, O = 2, N_free = 1) + tittle (a tiny blob — after pruning often a single pixel, O = 0 with zero edges, so emitted as a 'dot' stroke of length 0). Step 7 TSP orders stem-first because the stem's top is the highest starting point and the dot's start is even higher but the pen-up distance from dot-end to stem-start is the same as stem-end to dot-start. With the writing-order bias preferring to END at the bottom, the optimal sequence is stem-down-then-dot, which matches human cursive (italic 'i' is also dotted last). Print 'i' is sometimes dotted first; the bias coefficient lets us tune which.

Same component structure as 'i': stem (O = 2, one trail) + tittle (O = 0, dot). The stem is curved at the bottom but still a simple path in the graph — Hierholzer traces it as one trail from top of stem to tail-tip. TSP picks stem-then-dot for the same reason as 'i'. Stem direction is top→tail-tip by writing-order penalty (top is the higher endpoint).

pitfalls: Honest self-critique: (1) MINIMUM TRAILS IS NOT HUMAN. The biggest blind spot of the pure graph-theoretic view is that humans don't minimize stroke count or retracing — they follow motor-control conventions. 'm' is the cleanest counter-example: minimum-retrace says 2 trails, humans say 1 trail with retraces. The algorithm needs an external N_target policy (the LETTER_STRATEGY map analog), at which point the T-join machinery does the right thing — but choosing N_target is back to per-letter taste. The graph theory removes the geometric heuristics but does not remove the writing-convention prior. (2) PAIRING THE ODD VERTICES IS THE WHOLE GAME. For O = 4 there are 3 pairings; for O = 6, 15; for O = 8, 105. The writing_order_penalty I sketched is a soft heuristic dressed in math notation — calling it a 'cost function' doesn't make it principled. A more honest formulation: the pairing must be learned from a dataset of human-written letters, or the algorithm degenerates back to heuristics with a graph-theoretic veneer. (3) THE SKELETON IS NOT THE LETTER. Medial-axis skeletons of bold fonts produce spurious branches (serif spurs, ink-trap notches) that survive pruning. Hierholzer obediently traces every spur as part of a trail, producing strokes that visit serifs in the middle of a long downstroke — wrong for handwriting. We need a pre-Hierholzer step that classifies edges as 'structural' vs 'decorative' and either drops decorative edges or treats them as forced retraces — neither is pure graph theory. (4) JUNCTION-LOCAL TANGENT MATTERS, AND HIERHOLZER IS BLIND TO IT. At a degree-4 junction (crossing of two strokes), Hierholzer picks an arbitrary edge to leave on. The human picks the edge that continues the incoming tangent (straight-through over right-angle turn). Fixing this requires modifying Hierholzer to prefer collinear continuations — equivalent to the 'transition system' formulation of Eulerian decomposition (Kotzig 1968). This is doable but is the place where graph theory meets geometry and the clean abstraction breaks. (5) CLOSED COMPONENTS WITHOUT JUNCTIONS NEED A SYNTHETIC CUT NODE. Pure cycles like 'o' have no degree-≠2 vertices, so skeleton_to_graph as currently written produces an empty node set; we must inject a synthetic anchor. Not hard, but easy to forget and causes a silent empty-output bug. (6) T-JOIN VIA MIN-WEIGHT MATCHING IS POLYNOMIAL BUT NOT TRIVIAL. networkx.min_weight_matching is correct but slow on dense complete graphs; for letters with O > 10 (rare but possible in calligraphic faces with many serifs) it could be the bottleneck. (7) NO HANDLING OF DIRECTED STROKES. Real handwriting has direction (up-strokes thinner than down-strokes); my decomposition produces undirected trails. Imposing direction is another optimization layer (each trail can be traversed two ways; choose by writing-order bias) — sketched in step 7 but not formalized.

perspective: Medial-axis topologist: treat each glyph as a planar multigraph G=(V,E) where the cleaned skeleton has degree-1 vertices (endpoints), degree-2 vertices (smooth interior, absorbed into edges), and degree>=3 vertices (junctions). Decomposition into pen strokes is a constrained Eulerian-walk-cover problem on G, biased by junction-local geometry (tangent continuity) and global writing conventions (top-down, left-to-right, verticals before crossbars). The key invariants to lean on are: number of connected components (handles dotted i/j and punctuation), the first Betti number b1(G_c)=|E_c|-|V_c|+1 per component (counts the closed loops, fixes 'o', 'B', 'A'), and the parity of vertex degrees inside each component (determines the minimum number of open walks needed by the Chinese Postman / T-join theorem).
algorithm_overview: Per glyph, work component-by-component. Inside each component, do four things in order. (1) Determine the minimum number of open walks that cover every edge without retracing, using the parity-of-degrees / T-join argument: if a component has 2k odd-degree vertices and Betti number b1, it needs max(k, b1>0 ? 1 : 0) walks at minimum (pure-loop components need exactly one closed walk; trees with 2k leaves need k walks; graphs with both loops and odd vertices need k walks but at least one walk must traverse each loop). (2) Choose how to "pair up" odd-degree vertices at each junction to define which incident edges belong to the same walk. This is a local matching problem at every degree>=3 vertex, solved by minimum-weight perfect matching where the weight is a geometric/handwriting cost (turn angle, parallel-edge penalty, "vertical-pass-through" bonus). For loops attached to a junction, this matching also decides where the loop is "cut" into a back-and-forth incident pair, which is what makes 'B' draw correctly. (3) Once pairings are fixed, the walk decomposition is determined: walk from each unpaired odd-degree leaf (or, for pure-loop components, from the topmost point) and follow paired transits through each junction until you exit at another leaf or return to the start. (4) Order and orient the resulting walks using the writing-order key (Y-band, then verticals-before-horizontals, then X). The non-trivial part is step 2; the rest is bookkeeping.

core_steps.name: Connected component split
core_steps.rationale: Multi-part glyphs (i, j, !, ?, :, ;, =) are several disconnected pieces in G. Each piece is its own decomposition problem; the only cross-component decision is final ordering. Components are also the unit at which Betti numbers and odd-vertex counts are meaningful.
core_steps.pseudocode:
components = list(nx.connected_components(G))
results = []
for C in components:
    Gc = G.subgraph(C).copy()
    walks_c = decompose_component(Gc, dist_map)
    results.extend(walks_c)
return order_walks(results)   # writing-order key, top-down, verticals first
core_steps.edge_cases: A noisy skeleton can yield tiny spurious components from pruning leftovers. Drop any component with fewer than k_min edges (k_min ~ 4 px of path length) before decomposing. Real dots (i, j, :) are blob-sized after rasterization; they survive the threshold. Punctuation like '?' has the curl-component plus a separate dot; both must be kept.

core_steps.name: Compute topological signature of component
core_steps.rationale: Before choosing walks, classify the component. Let L = {v : deg(v) == 1} (leaves), J = {v : deg(v) >= 3} (junctions). Let b1 = |E_c| - |V_after_smoothing_c| + 1 = number of independent loops. Number of odd-degree vertices is |L| plus odd-degree junctions. Min open walks by the T-join lower bound is max(1, |odd|/2) for connected non-Eulerian graphs; pure-loop components (|odd|==0, b1>=1) need exactly b1 closed walks if they share no vertices, else 1 walk that covers all of them (rarely the case for Latin).
core_steps.pseudocode:
leaves = [v for v in Gc if Gc.degree(v) == 1]
junctions = [v for v in Gc if Gc.degree(v) >= 3]
odd = [v for v in Gc if Gc.degree(v) % 2 == 1]
b1 = Gc.number_of_edges() - Gc.number_of_nodes() + 1   # connected
if len(odd) == 0:
    n_walks = 1                # pure cycle: o, O, single loop
else:
    n_walks = len(odd) // 2    # T-join lower bound
core_steps.edge_cases: A 'theta' shape (figure-8 of two loops joined at one junction) has |odd| = 0 but two loops at a degree-4 vertex; topologically Eulerian, but a person draws it as 2 strokes. Override: if b1 >= 2 and there exist degree>=4 junctions, allow splitting one Eulerian circuit into 2 walks at the junction the matching prefers. Also: a graph that is a single cycle plus a tail (lowercase 'a' single-story) has 2 odd vertices on the tail-end and b1==1; lower bound says 1 walk, and one walk indeed covers it (start at tail-end, walk to junction, walk around bowl, return). We accept that the lower bound walk count is what a person would draw.

core_steps.name: Local pairing at each junction (the core decision)
core_steps.rationale: For a degree-d junction v, the d incident edge-ends must be partitioned into pass-through pairs (each pair becomes part of the same walk) plus optionally one or two unpaired ends if the walk count requires it. This is a perfect (or near-perfect) matching on the d incident edge-ends. The cost of matching ends i and j is a sum of handwriting-aware penalties: (i) turn angle 180-theta_ij (straight-through = 0, U-turn = expensive); (ii) parallel-edge penalty if i and j are the two ends of the same multi-edge AND b1-around-them is 0 (this preserves bowls but discourages retracing thin parallel splits); (iii) writing-direction bonus that prefers pairings consistent with top-down vertical motion when one of the edges is near-vertical (matches the 'M' / 'N' / 'W' convention). Solve as min-cost perfect matching via networkx (Blossom).
core_steps.pseudocode:
def pair_junction(v, Gc, dist_map):
    incident = [(u, k, path) for (u, k, path) in edges_at[v]]  # d entries
    d = len(incident)
    tans = [tangent_at(path, v) for (u, k, path) in incident]
    # Build a complete graph on incident slots; weight = pairing cost.
    H = nx.Graph()
    for i in range(d):
        for j in range(i+1, d):
            ti, tj = tans[i], tans[j]
            # 1) Turn-angle cost. Two outgoing tangents point AWAY from v.
            #    Continuation -> dot product close to -1. cost = 1 + dot.
            angle_cost = 1.0 + float(np.dot(ti, tj))     # [0, 2]
            # 2) Same-edge (multi-edge) penalty unless it is a self-loop bowl.
            same_multi = incident[i][:2] == incident[j][:2]   # (neighbor, key)
            multi_cost = 0.0
            if same_multi and not is_real_bowl(incident[i][2], dist_map):
                multi_cost = 2.0   # heavily discourage retracing parallel splits
            # 3) Vertical-pass-through bonus.
            vert_i = abs(ti[0]) > 0.85;  vert_j = abs(tj[0]) > 0.85
            same_vert_chain = (vert_i and vert_j and ti[0] * tj[0] < 0)
            vert_bonus = -0.4 if same_vert_chain else 0.0
            H.add_edge(i, j, weight=angle_cost + multi_cost + vert_bonus)
    if d % 2 == 0:
        matching = nx.min_weight_matching(H, maxcardinality=True)
    else:
        # Add a dummy slot connected to all real slots with cost = LEAF_COST.
        H.add_node('dummy')
        for i in range(d):
            H.add_edge(i, 'dummy', weight=LEAF_COST)
        matching = nx.min_weight_matching(H, maxcardinality=True)
        matching = {(a, b) for (a, b) in matching if 'dummy' not in (a, b)}
    return matching, incident
core_steps.edge_cases: Self-loops at v (a bowl that returns to the same junction, e.g. lowercase 'b' bowl, lowercase 'a' bowl) appear as two incident edge-ends i and j with the same neighbor==v and same key. The same-multi-edge rule must NOT penalise these — `is_real_bowl` should test (a) the path is long compared to dist_map's local width and (b) the path encloses an area larger than the threshold used in collapse_parallel_edges. A degree-3 junction (T, Y) has an odd number of ends; the dummy slot in the matching represents the one end that will start or terminate a walk. The matching is allowed to leave more than one slot unpaired if 'dummy' wins multiple times — set the dummy multiplicity to (d - 2*n_through) where n_through is desired pass-through count = floor(d/2) for forced single-walk components; for components where n_walks > 1 we increase the dummy multiplicity by 2*(n_walks_local - 1).

core_steps.name: Walk assembly
core_steps.rationale: After every junction's pairing is fixed, the union forms a 2-regular structure on the 'edge-end' graph (every edge-end is connected to exactly one other edge-end either by walking along its edge to the other side, or by the junction-local pairing decision). Connected components of this structure are exactly the strokes. Walks are obtained by traversal: start at any unpaired edge-end (leaf or matching-dummy slot), follow alternating edge-traversals and junction-pairings until you reach another unpaired end or return to start.
core_steps.edge_cases: Pure-cycle components ('o', 'O') have no unpaired ends; treat them like trace_closed_loops does — start at the topmost pixel, go clockwise. A degree-4 junction with two pass-through pairs (cross of 'x' or 't') produces a single walk only if the two pairings happen to chain through the same global cycle; in general it produces two separate walks (one per pair), which is what we want for 'x' (two diagonals).

core_steps.name: Walk ordering and orientation
core_steps.rationale: Final ordering should approximate Latin handwriting convention: top-down into Y-bands of ~60 px (canvas-relative), within each band verticals before crossbars (a person writes the upright before the crossbar in 't', 'A', 'H'), within ties left-to-right. Orientation per walk: verticals top->bottom; horizontals left->right; cycles already start at topmost.
core_steps.edge_cases: Cycles that span multiple bands (the bowl of 'B') want to be drawn AFTER the spine, regardless of where their topmost point sits. Override the band rule for walks whose topology is a closed loop: assign them the band of the JUNCTION through which they attach, not the band of their topmost pixel. For free-standing cycles ('o', 'O'), the band of the topmost pixel is correct.

handles_letters.notes: Lower bound is 1 closed walk. Skip to step 4 pure-cycle path; start at topmost pixel, walk clockwise. No matching needed.
Two leaves, no junctions. Matching is trivial. Walk from top leaf to bottom leaf, oriented top->bottom.

handles_letters.topology_class: 2-component (stem + dot); stem is single-line, dot is tiny cycle or single point
handles_letters.notes: Component split yields stem (b1=0, |odd|=2, 1 walk) and dot (b1=1 if rasterized as ring, else 0; |odd|=0 in either case, treated as 1 walk). Order key places stem first (lower band, vertical), then dot above? In practice the dot's ymin is smaller than the stem's ymin so the dot would sort first by band. Fix in step 5: prefer 'main vertical before isolated dot' by treating any component whose total path length is below STEM_FRACTION*max_component_length as an after-thought and pushing it to the END of the ordering. This is how people write i: stem first, dot last.
Same as 'i' but the stem component has |odd|=2 (top + tail), b1=0. Single walk from top to tail. Dot is appended last by the small-component override.

handles_letters.topology_class: single-component cross (b1=0, |odd|=4 — top of stem, bottom of stem, left of bar, right of bar; 1 degree-4 junction)
handles_letters.notes: Lower bound |odd|/2 = 2 walks. At the junction the matching pairs (top-stem, bottom-stem) via straight-vertical bonus, and (left-bar, right-bar) as the only remaining option. Walk 1: stem top->bottom. Walk 2: bar left->right. Ordering: band rule puts stem first (taller, lower ymin if t has descender), verticals-before-horizontals breaks ties; bar is drawn last. This matches handwriting.

handles_letters.topology_class: single-component triangle-with-crossbar (b1=1, 2 degree-3 junctions, |odd|=2 — the two feet)
handles_letters.notes: Lower bound is 1 (|odd|/2 = 1). But the convention for 'A' is to draw the two diagonal legs as one inverted V, then the crossbar — that's 2 strokes. With Betti number = 1, the graph IS Eulerian-trail-capable in 1 walk (foot -> apex -> down to one junction -> crossbar -> other junction -> down to other foot), so the topological lower bound is wrong relative to handwriting. The matching at each degree-3 junction picks (leg-down, crossbar) as a leaf-pair if we add a small bonus for 'leave the loop at a junction with a horizontal partner'. Better: special-case the override 'closed-loop on top of a baseline' (test: b1==1 AND the loop's bounding box is in the upper 70% of the component AND the two feet are at the bottom) — force the matching to put both crossbar-ends as dummy-matched, generating exactly 2 walks (V-shape + crossbar). This is the one place where pure topology underestimates and a writing-convention override is required.

handles_letters.topology_class: single-component, b1=2 (two bowls), 1 degree-4 junction on the spine where both bowls meet plus 2 degree-3 junctions (spine top, spine bottom)
handles_letters.notes: Realistically the cleaned skeleton of B has spine top, spine middle (degree-4: spine-up, spine-down, top-bowl-end, bottom-bowl-end), spine bottom, and the two bowls as self-loops at top and middle (top bowl) and at middle and bottom (bottom bowl). |odd|: leaves are spine-top and spine-bottom (degree 1 if bowls don't touch them; usually degree 2 or 3 depending on serif). Lower-bound walk count = max(1, |odd|/2) but b1=2 means at least 2 walks because a single walk can include at most one return-to-start. Matching at the degree-4 middle junction prefers (spine-up, spine-down) straight-through; bowls become two self-loops to be traversed as separate walks. Result: walk 1 spine top->bottom, walks 2&3 the two bowls. Ordering: spine first (vertical, leftmost), then upper bowl, then lower bowl. This is 3 walks — slightly more than the canonical 2, but acceptable and matches some handwriting styles. To collapse to 2 walks (spine, then one continuous bowl-bowl curve), add a matching rule at the middle junction: 'if two self-loops are present, prefer matching their incident ends to each other to chain bowls into one walk'. That's a configurable preference.

handles_letters.topology_class: single-component, b1=1 (one bowl), 1 degree-3 junction on the stem
handles_letters.notes: Stem has top leaf, joins bowl at one junction, bowl is a self-loop at that junction. |odd|=2 (the top leaf and the implicit 'half-degree' at the junction — actually junction has degree 3 = stem + 2 bowl-ends = odd). At the junction the matching chooses to pair (bowl-end-A, bowl-end-B) as straight pass-through (continuing around the bowl), leaving stem-end as the dummy partner. Walk: top of stem -> down to junction -> around bowl back to junction -> stop. One walk, matches handwriting. Good case.

handles_letters.topology_class: single-component, b1=0 (no enclosed area), 2 degree-3 junctions (where outer legs meet inner V), |odd|=4 (the 4 feet/peaks: 2 outer bottoms, 2 outer tops)
handles_letters.notes: Wait — M has 4 endpoints (two outer bottoms at baseline, but the outer top peaks are degree-3 junctions). Recount: bottom-left foot, top-left peak (deg 3), valley bottom (deg 2), top-right peak (deg 3), bottom-right foot. Leaves = 2 (the two feet). |odd|=2. Lower bound = 1 walk. Matching at top-left peak: pairs (up-from-leg, down-to-valley) as the straight-through option (small turn angle), leaving the outer-up tangent unpaired? No — top-left peak is degree-3 (incoming left leg, going down toward valley, going down toward outer-top is the leg itself). Actually for M the typical skeleton has 5 segments meeting at 2 junctions inside the top. The pairing chooses left-leg <-> inner-down-V and outer-leg <-> nothing, but if outer-leg is the 'up' part, the matching prefers it paired with the leg coming up from the bottom. Net result: one zigzag walk bottom-left -> top-left -> valley -> top-right -> bottom-right. This is what a person draws.

handles_letters.topology_class: single-component, b1=0, 2 degree-3 junctions on the top hump-line, |odd|=6 (3 feet at the bottom plus top-of-3-humps... no, the humps are smooth)
handles_letters.notes: Lowercase m has 3 vertical legs joined by 2 humps at the top. Skeleton: 3 leaves at the bottom (3 feet) + 2 degree-3 junctions where each hump meets the next leg. |odd|=3+2=5; that's odd which is impossible (handshaking lemma) so re-examine: at each top-junction, degree=3 (leg up, hump-left curve, hump-right curve). So junctions contribute 2 odd vertices. Leaves contribute 3. Total odd=5 — still odd. The 5th odd must be the topmost point of the first hump, which would actually be a smooth-degree-2 point along the leftmost hump. Recount: leaves=3 feet; junctions=2 (degree 3 each); total odd=5 — violates handshaking, so my topology is wrong. Reality: the first leg's top is itself a leaf or a degree-2 point that turns into the first hump. So leaves=3 feet PLUS the top of the first leg = 4 leaves. Total odd = 4 + 2 = 6, lower bound = 3 walks. But people draw 'm' in one or two strokes. The classic convention: stroke 1 = leftmost leg down, stroke 2 = top-of-leg arc to second-leg, etc., depending on style. Honest answer: 3 walks topologically minimum, the user's preferred 1-walk-cursive 'm' requires retracing. We accept retracing here OR we mark this glyph as one where the user-preferred stroke count exceeds the topological lower bound and document it. The algorithm prints 3 walks; the user-facing pipeline can post-merge contiguous walks at smooth-tangent junctions if a lower stroke count is desired.

handles_letters.topology_class: single-component, b1=0, 1 degree-3 junction (where the two arms meet the stem), |odd|=4 (top of stem, bottom of stem, end of upper arm, end of lower arm)
handles_letters.notes: Lower bound = 2 walks. Matching at the junction (degree 3) pairs (stem-up, stem-down) as straight-through (vertical bonus), leaving the arm-into-junction end as the dummy. Plus the OTHER arm — wait, k's junction has degree 3 not 4: stem segments contribute 2 ends (up + down from the join), and BOTH arms together contribute 1 (because they share a node at the join). If the upper arm and the lower arm meet the stem at the SAME junction node (which they do after junction-cluster-merge), that node is degree 4 (stem-up, stem-down, upper-arm, lower-arm). |odd|=4 leaves; lower bound = 2 walks. Matching: (stem-up, stem-down) straight-through, (upper-arm, lower-arm) is the only remaining option — but those two go roughly NE and SE, dot product ~ -0.5, not straight-through but workable. Walk 1: stem top->bottom. Walk 2: upper-arm-tip -> junction -> lower-arm-tip. The matching gets this right because the vertical bonus dominates the slightly-bent arm chain.

pitfalls: There are five honest weaknesses in this approach. (1) The topological lower bound underestimates 'A': pure-Euler-trail logic says 1 walk, but humans draw 2. We need a writing-convention override for "closed loop sitting on two legs" (A, R, possibly K-with-bowl). Without it the algorithm reduces 'A' to a single retrace-free walk that traces V, then crossbar, then descends inside the loop — which is topologically valid but looks alien. Diagnosing when the override applies requires non-local geometry (the bowl is "above" the legs); that's a heuristic on top of the algorithm. (2) The topological lower bound OVERESTIMATES 'm' and 'w' relative to cursive convention. Topology says 3 walks for m (4 leaves => 2 walks per T-join, plus the dangling top); a cursive m is one stroke with smooth turns. The only way to get 1-stroke m is to allow controlled retracing, which violates the "no retrace" goal. The algorithm gives the correct minimal non-retracing count; documenting that as a design choice is important. (3) Bowl-vs-medial-split detection at matching time depends on `is_real_bowl`, which currently reuses the dist_map/area test from `collapse_parallel_edges`. If the upstream collapse already merged a real bowl by mistake, the matching sees no self-loop and decomposes incorrectly with no way to recover. The algorithm is only as good as the cleaned graph that feeds it. (4) Degree-4+ junctions with two valid orthogonal pairings (the crossing of 'x', 't') always have a tie: both (NE,SW) + (NW,SE) and (NE,NW) + (SW,SE) cost zero by tangent alone. The pairing must break ties by writing convention (verticals chained first), which is brittle for skew or rotated fonts. (5) The min-weight matching with dummy slots only enforces an EVEN number of unpaired ends; it cannot independently set per-junction walk counts. If the global walk count needs to differ from what local matchings produce, we must run a global pass that adjusts dummy multiplicities — a hairy optimization. In practice we solve locally and accept the resulting walk count. The Hershey-template approach side-steps all five of these by importing human-authored decompositions; the cost is loss of generality, which is exactly the trade-off this project is reconsidering.

perspective: Motor-control neuroscientist specialising in handwriting kinematics. I treat a glyph as a motor program: a sequence of ballistic strokes, each one a single accelerate-decelerate pen sweep. Topology (what walks cover the graph) and kinematics (what a writer actually does) are different problems; the algorithm must solve topology first, then bias the topological choice using motor cost.
algorithm_overview: Treat the pruned skeleton as a multigraph and pose decomposition as a minimum-cost Chinese Postman / route-inspection variant. For each connected component independently: (1) classify the component by its odd-degree-vertex count and cycle structure into one of a small set of motor topologies; (2) solve the T-join problem (which odd vertices to pair, hence which edges to either retrace or pen-lift across) using a motor cost that weighs retrace vs lift-and-restart; (3) extract walks by Hierholzer's algorithm on the augmented multigraph; (4) cut each Eulerian walk at high-curvature "corner" vertices where a real writer would stop and re-launch; (5) order and orient the resulting walks by a handwriting-bias score (topmost-leftmost free endpoint first, verticals before horizontals, prefer downstrokes over upstrokes, prefer leftward-to-rightward sweeps). The key motor insight encoded throughout: pen-lift cost L is large, retrace cost R(d) grows with distance, and corner cost C(theta) is convex in turn angle — so the algorithm prefers smooth long walks, accepts short retraces, and lifts only when forced.

core_steps.name: Component split and contraction
core_steps.rationale: Multi-component glyphs (i, j, !, ?, :, ;) are independent motor sub-programs. Inside one component, degree-2 chains are just shape, not decisions, so we contract them into single weighted edges to keep the combinatorics small. Edge weight = arc length; we also stash the polyline geometry for later.
core_steps.edge_cases: Self-loops (bowl of lowercase 'a' after junction merging) become MultiGraph self-edges with degree contribution 2; keep them as-is. Spur shorter than ~3px is skeleton noise — drop before this step. A component with a single endpoint is impossible on a clean skeleton; if it occurs, the skeletonizer is buggy and we log.

core_steps.name: Motor-topology classification
core_steps.rationale: Before optimisation, classify what kind of glyph we are looking at — it tells us the lower bound on stroke count and what the writer's natural decomposition will be. The classification is from graph invariants alone, not from the letter identity.
core_steps.pseudocode:
def classify(H):
    if H.kind == 'loop':         return 'CLOSED_LOOP'   # o, O, counter of D
    odd = [v for v in H if H.degree(v) % 2 == 1]
    cyc = H.number_of_edges() - H.number_of_nodes() + 1  # cyclomatic number
    if not odd and cyc == 1:     return 'CLOSED_LOOP'
    if not odd and cyc >= 2:     return 'MULTI_LOOP'    # theta, 8
    if len(odd) == 2 and cyc == 0: return 'OPEN_LINE'   # l, /, S, C
    if len(odd) == 2 and cyc >= 1: return 'LINE_WITH_LOOP'  # b, d, p, q, 6, 9
    if len(odd) >= 4 and cyc == 0: return 'TREE'        # T, Y, k, t, F, E, H, A skeleton without bowl
    return 'MIXED'                                       # A, B, R, M, m, W, K
core_steps.edge_cases: Junction-merge artefacts can change odd-count parity; run merge BEFORE classification. Letters 'A' and 'R' often classify as MIXED because the bowl gives one cycle while the legs give odd vertices. Self-loops contribute even degree, so a 'b' is correctly OPEN_LINE if we ignore the loop edge or LINE_WITH_LOOP if we keep it — keep it.

core_steps.name: T-join: pick which odd vertices to pair
core_steps.rationale: Chinese Postman result: a graph has an Eulerian walk iff at most 2 odd-degree vertices; otherwise we must either retrace some edges (turning odd into even) OR break into multiple walks (each walk consumes 2 odd vertices as its endpoints). A writer chooses between these per pair based on motor cost: short retrace beats pen-lift, long retrace loses to pen-lift. Solve as min-cost perfect matching on the odd-vertex set, with three edge-cost options per pair.
core_steps.pseudocode:
L = pen_lift_cost                      # large positive constant, ~150 px equiv
ALPHA = 0.6                            # retrace penalty multiplier (each retraced unit length counts as ALPHA * length of motor effort)
MAX_RETRACE = 0.35 * total_edge_length(H)  # never retrace more than 35% of the glyph

def pair_cost(u, v, H):
    d_short = shortest_path_length(H, u, v)
    if d_short <= MAX_RETRACE:
        retrace = ALPHA * d_short      # walk uses these edges twice
    else:
        retrace = +inf
    lift = L + euclid(u, v)            # pen-up cost + air travel
    return min(retrace, lift), 'retrace' if retrace < lift else 'lift'

def solve_tjoin(H, odd):
    # complete graph on odd vertices, edge weight = pair_cost
    K = nx.Graph()
    for u, v in combinations(odd, 2):
        c, kind = pair_cost(u, v, H)
        K.add_edge(u, v, weight=c, kind=kind)
    matching = nx.algorithms.matching.min_weight_matching(K)
    return matching                    # set of (u,v) pairs
core_steps.edge_cases: Odd count must be even (handshake lemma). For glyphs with very large odd count (E has 4, k has 4) we sometimes prefer pen-lift on EVERY pair: this naturally yields the expected (#odd)/2 strokes plus loop strokes. ALPHA and L are calibrated so a 1-cell retrace beats a lift but a 60-px retrace does not. Closed loops have no odd vertices but still need a 'virtual' start, handled in step 5.

core_steps.name: Augment and Eulerian decomposition
core_steps.rationale: Once we know which odd pairs to retrace, doubling those edges (or rather the shortest path between them) makes the graph have exactly 2k odd vertices where k = number of 'lift' pairs. Hierholzer then yields k Eulerian walks, each entering one odd of a lift-pair and exiting another.
core_steps.edge_cases: Hierholzer on a disconnected augmented graph after partial removal: re-check connectivity each iteration. If the matching's lift pair leaves no path in A between the endpoints, fall back to retracing — should be rare since min-cost matching already chose retrace when possible.

core_steps.name: Kinematic cut at high-curvature corners
core_steps.rationale: Topology says a walk can be one stroke; motor control says a corner sharper than ~75 degrees forces a velocity zero-crossing, which IS a stroke boundary. Cutting after topology rather than before respects what writers actually do (e.g. 'M' is topologically a 4-edge tree that can be one Eulerian walk, but a writer makes 3 or 4 strokes through it).
core_steps.pseudocode:
THETA_CUT = math.radians(75)

def cut_at_corners(walk):
    pieces, cur = [], [walk[0]]
    for i in range(1, len(walk) - 1):
        cur.append(walk[i])
        t_in  = unit(walk[i] - walk[i-1])     # tangent estimated over ~10 px window for noise
        t_out = unit(walk[i+1] - walk[i])
        if math.acos(clip(dot(t_in, t_out), -1, 1)) >= THETA_CUT:
            pieces.append(cur); cur = [walk[i]]
    cur.append(walk[-1]); pieces.append(cur)
    # Don't cut if the corner is the only feature (would explode 'l' tail-flick)
    pieces = [p for p in pieces if length(p) >= MIN_STROKE_LEN]
    return pieces
core_steps.edge_cases: M and W generate 3-4 cuts as expected; the cusp at the bottom of 'V' generates 2 strokes which is what writers do. 'O' has no corner above threshold so cut never fires (good). For cursive joins, THETA_CUT can be relaxed; for printed fonts 75 deg is right. Tangent estimation must use a smoothing window (~8-12 px) or skeleton aliasing fires spurious cuts.

core_steps.name: Handwriting-order biasing of starts and orientations
core_steps.rationale: Handwriting bias: start at the topmost-leftmost free endpoint of the first stroke; if no endpoints, start at top of a closed loop and go clockwise (English convention) or counter-clockwise (Hebrew/Arabic). Within a glyph, strokes execute top-to-bottom, left-to-right; verticals before horizontals at equal Y (the crossbar of 't' is drawn after the stem). Apply this AFTER topology+cuts so we don't bias topology choice itself.
core_steps.edge_cases: For lowercase 'i' the dot is drawn AFTER the stem in modern handwriting but historically before; we pick after by sorting on Y first (stem top is above the dot only if the dot is itself a small component above x-height — which it is). The crossbar of 't' must come after the stem: handled by `vertical-first` flag. Cursive ligatures break left-to-right; out of scope here.

core_steps.name: Closed-loop and multi-loop handling
core_steps.rationale: A pure loop has no odd vertices and no natural endpoints. The writer picks a launch point and a direction. Use topmost pixel + clockwise for English. A theta-like multi-loop (figure 8, lower-case 'B' as two stacked loops without serifs) needs 2 Eulerian circuits sharing one vertex — the writer either lifts between or retraces a small bridge; choose by motor cost as in step 3.
core_steps.edge_cases: '8' written as one stroke crosses itself at the pinch and is topologically one Eulerian circuit — but kinematically two strokes because the corner at the pinch exceeds THETA_CUT. The corner-cut step handles this for free, so the algorithm need not special-case 8.

handles_letters.notes: Single connected component, no odd vertices, cyclomatic 1. Step 6 picks topmost pixel as start, orients clockwise. One smooth walk, no corners above 75 deg, no cuts. Matches kinematic expectation.

Two endpoints (top, bottom). Eulerian path between them, one walk. Step 6 picks topmost (top) as start, draws top-to-bottom downstroke. Coverage metric bug for narrow letters is irrelevant to topology.

Stem = OPEN_LINE (1 walk, top-down). Dot = CLOSED_LOOP or tiny line (1 walk). Step 6 sorts: stem-top Y < dot Y? No, dot is above stem; but our convention (modern Latin handwriting) draws stem first, then dot. Override: components whose bounding box is fully above x-height AND have small area are scheduled LAST. This is the one acceptable per-script tweak.

Like 'i' but stem has a hook descender. Stem still classifies as OPEN_LINE (two endpoints: top of stem, bottom of hook). Step 5 may cut at the hook curve if the curvature exceeds threshold — for most fonts the hook is smooth and we get 1 walk for the stem + 1 for the dot.

handles_letters.topology_class: MIXED (LINE_WITH_LOOP or TREE depending on font)
handles_letters.notes: Skeleton: two legs meet at apex, crossbar inside. Odd vertices: 2 leg feet (degree 1) + 2 crossbar ends (degree 1 inside) = 4 odd. Cyclomatic = 1 (triangle formed by apex + two crossbar junctions). Min-cost matching: pair (left-foot, right-foot) → must lift across the figure (long lift); pair (left-crossbar, right-crossbar) → short retrace possible. So solver chooses: 1 walk from apex down left leg then up apex then down right leg (would require apex degree-2 traversal once — actually apex has degree 2 if legs meet there, or degree 4 if crossbar attaches at apex). For typical sans-serif A: apex degree 2, two crossbar junctions degree 3 each. Solver produces: stroke 1 = left leg (apex → foot), stroke 2 = right leg (apex → foot), stroke 3 = crossbar — 3 walks. Matches the standard 3-stroke A taught in schools.

handles_letters.topology_class: TREE / MIXED depending on apex shape
handles_letters.notes: Skeleton has 2 endpoints (feet) and either 2 or 3 internal junctions. As a tree with exactly 2 odd vertices it admits one Eulerian walk: foot-up-down-up-down-foot. BUT three 75 deg corners at the inner peaks force step 5 to cut into 3-4 strokes. This is the key example of topology=1 / kinematics=many. My algorithm correctly produces 4 strokes (left up, inner V down-up, then last leg down) without any letter-specific code.

Lowercase m has 2 endpoints (left foot, right foot) and arches between. Eulerian path exists. Two arches mean two ~120 deg downward turns — these are BELOW the 75 deg cut threshold (turn angle measured as deviation from straight, so a smooth arch is ~30 deg per segment). So step 5 does NOT cut, producing one continuous walk. This matches cursive m but NOT print m (where writers draw 3 strokes). To get print-style 3-stroke m I'd lower THETA_CUT to ~50 deg for serif-style classification — explicit knob, not hidden heuristic.

Stem + bowl joined at top and bottom of bowl. Two odd vertices (top of stem, bottom of bowl join) plus one cycle. Eulerian path exists between the two odd vertices: stem-down then around bowl. Step 6 starts at top of stem. No corner above 75 deg (bowl is smooth, junctions inside bowl are smooth tangent). One walk. Matches one-stroke 'b'.

Spine + two stacked bowls. Odd vertices: top of spine, bottom of spine = 2 odd. Cycles: 2 (upper bowl, lower bowl). Topologically Eulerian as 1 walk! But step 5 cuts at the sharp middle-junction reverse where the spine meets both bowls (turn-angle ~180 deg at the middle waist). Result: 2 walks (spine top→bottom, then both bowls as one Eulerian circuit, OR spine + each bowl). My matching solver actually prefers the 2-stroke decomposition because the implied 'retrace' through the middle joint is short — so cost of the 1-walk topology is high. Honest assessment: this is the borderline case my algorithm may get wrong if I tune ALPHA carelessly.

Stem with a crossbar = T-junction (degree 3) plus 3 endpoints (top of stem, two ends of crossbar). Odd vertices = 4. Min-cost matching: pair (top-stem, bottom-stem-implied) doesn't exist because stem bottom IS an endpoint. Actually endpoints are: top-of-stem, bottom-of-stem, left-crossbar, right-crossbar. Matching pairs: (top, bottom) — lift trivially if both in same long path, (left, right) — short retrace through junction. Min-cost picks 2 walks via 2 lifts: stroke 1 = stem (top to bottom), stroke 2 = crossbar (left to right). Step 6 orders vertical-first, so stem comes before crossbar. Matches printed 't' exactly.

Stem + two diagonal legs meeting at a midpoint junction. 4 odd vertices (3 endpoints of stem/legs + 1 stem bottom). Min-cost matching favours 2 strokes: stem (top→bottom) and diagonals (upper-right→junction→lower-right, possibly with a small retrace at junction OR with corner cut). For lowercase k, the junction angle between the two diagonals is typically ~60-90 deg, so step 5 may or may not cut. Honest: my algorithm produces 2 strokes (stem + a single V for the diagonals) — many writers draw k as 3 strokes (stem, upper-diagonal, lower-diagonal). To recover 3-stroke k, I'd need a per-script convention table — not a topology change.

pitfalls: "Pitfalls and honest self-critique. (1) The matching cost ALPHA and lift cost L are global constants but the right balance is font-dependent and even letter-dependent: a bold sans-serif retraces feel cheaper (more pigment hides the doubling) than a fine script. Tuning these to make A come out 3-stroke may simultaneously make B come out 1-stroke and break it. (2) Step 5's curvature threshold THETA_CUT is the single biggest hidden lever. At 75 deg, 'm' is one cursive sweep — wrong for print fonts. At 50 deg, 'S' breaks into 2-3 pieces — wrong for everything. The honest fix is a per-font calibration pass, not a constant. (3) The algorithm is silent on ductus where it matters most: it cannot tell that 'E' in printed form is 4 strokes (spine + 3 horizontals, each drawn left-to-right) versus 1 Eulerian zig-zag. Topology allows the zig-zag; my corner cuts catch most of it but the bottom-left and top-left corners are exactly at threshold. I would need an explicit 'serif-corner' prior. (4) Closed-loop direction (cw vs ccw) is hard-coded as cw for Latin. This is wrong for 'o' in cursive (often ccw starting from upper-right) and very wrong for Arabic/Hebrew scripts. The algorithm should ingest a per-script convention rather than a global constant. (5) Min-weight matching is O(V^3); fine for V<=10 odd vertices but a glyph like '@' or a complex ligature could have 20+ — would need approximation. (6) I assume the skeleton is clean; the algorithm has zero defense against junction-merge errors that flip a vertex's parity. Robustness needs an explicit 'integrate over plausible merges' which I have not specified. (7) Letters where my algorithm is most likely wrong: K (almost certainly 1 stroke topologically, but writers do 3), B (borderline as noted), E (will produce a Eulerian zig-zag instead of 4 strokes unless THETA_CUT is tight), Z (will be one walk — actually correct for cursive but writers of print Z lift). (8) Most fundamental limit: I am using only graph structure + curvature. A real writer uses muscle-group economy (don't ask the hand to draw against its anatomy) and learned motor schemata. Without those priors the algorithm cannot tell that horizontal strokes are easier left-to-right for right-handers, that descenders are pulled rather than pushed, and that an 'X' is two diagonals not one zig-zag — these are conventions, not consequences of graph theory."

perspective: Pragmatic Python engineer (numpy/networkx/scipy) replacing the Hershey-template tracer with a graph-theoretic one. Optimised for a <300-line implementation that consumes the existing skeleton + pixel graph + distance field, and emits a list of walks per connected component. The whole thing is fundamentally a Chinese-Postman-like edge-cover problem on a small (≤a few thousand pixels), planar, integer-coordinate graph — so I'm leaning on classical algorithms (Hierholzer + odd-pair matching) rather than heuristic stroke-merging, with one carefully bounded pre-processing step (junction contraction) and one carefully bounded post-processing step (oriented stroke splitting at junctions) to make the result match handwriting intuition.
algorithm_overview: The medial-axis skeleton, after pruning and junction-merging, is a small planar multigraph G. The question "what are the strokes?" is *almost* "what is the Eulerian decomposition of G?" — every edge must be walked, retracing should be minimal, and we want as few walks as possible. That makes this a Chinese-Postman / T-join problem. The minimum number of open walks needed to cover every edge of a connected graph equals max(1, odd_degree_nodes / 2); adding the right matching edges between odd-degree nodes turns it Eulerian and lets us read off the walks with Hierholzer. The pieces that make this actually behave like handwriting are: (1) contracting the pixel graph G_pix into a "skeleton graph" G_skel whose nodes are endpoints and merged junctions and whose edges carry the underlying pixel path; (2) choosing the T-join (odd-pair pairing) with edge weights that prefer joining "naturally curved" continuations — so a horizontal+vertical stroke at a T-junction is preferred to a U-turn; (3) at each junction, when multiple Eulerian arcs pass through, splitting them into separate walks if the tangent angle change is sharp (>~110°) — this is what turns one Eulerian circuit through 'M' into four strokes. Components are processed independently; closed components (every node even, like 'o') use Hierholzer directly to produce one circuit; open components with k odd nodes produce ceil(k/2) walks.

core_steps.name: Build the skeleton graph G_skel
core_steps.rationale: The pixel-level graph has thousands of nodes and most decisions only happen at endpoints and junctions. Compressing degree-2 chains into edges (preserving the underlying pixel path as edge attribute `pixels`) gives us a graph with O(n_junctions + n_endpoints) nodes — typically <20 per glyph. This is the existing `skeleton_to_graph` + `merge_nearby_junctions` + `collapse_parallel_edges` output, so we reuse it as-is.
core_steps.pseudocode:
def build_skel_graph(skel, dist_map):
    G_pix = build_skel_pixel_graph(skel)            # existing
    G = skeleton_to_graph(skel)                     # existing, MultiGraph
    G = merge_nearby_junctions(G, max_dist=22)      # existing
    G = collapse_parallel_edges(G, dist_map)        # existing
    # G is a MultiGraph; nodes are (y,x) tuples; each edge has 'path'
    # (list of (y,x) pixel coords from u to v inclusive).
    for u, v, k, d in G.edges(keys=True, data=True):
        d['length']  = polyline_length(d['path'])
        d['tan_u']   = unit_tangent(d['path'], at='start')   # outward from u
        d['tan_v']   = unit_tangent(d['path'], at='end')     # outward from v
    return G
core_steps.edge_cases: Empty skeleton (whitespace glyph) -> return []. Single-pixel component -> emit a trivial 1-point walk. Self-loops (real closed bowls of 'a','p','q') are preserved as edges where u==v with a non-trivial path; tangents at u differ at the two ends of the loop, which the matching step needs to know about.

core_steps.name: Split into connected components
core_steps.rationale: Multi-part glyphs ('i', 'j', '!', ':', ';', '?', '=') are k separate connected subgraphs and you write each as its own pen-down/pen-up sequence. Per-component processing also keeps the matching problem small.
core_steps.pseudocode:
def decompose(skel, dist_map):
    G = build_skel_graph(skel, dist_map)
    walks = []
    for comp_nodes in nx.connected_components(G):
        Gc = G.subgraph(comp_nodes).copy()
        walks.extend(decompose_component(Gc))
    walks = order_walks_for_handwriting(walks)      # top-to-bottom, left-to-right
    return walks
core_steps.edge_cases: A component with zero edges (single isolated pixel) -> emit a length-0 walk so the renderer still places a dot. Components are returned in the standard handwriting order: top-to-bottom of bounding-box top, then left-to-right — this is what makes 'i' produce [stem, dot] rather than [dot, stem].

core_steps.name: Compute odd-degree set T and the minimum T-join matching
core_steps.rationale: Chinese Postman on a graph with k odd-degree nodes: you need ceil(k/2) open walks to cover all edges without retracing, OR you pair up the k odd nodes (a perfect matching in the complete graph K_T weighted by shortest-path-in-G distance) and the resulting matching tells you which odd nodes to treat as start/end of distinct walks vs which pairs to bridge with a retrace. For open-walk decomposition (we don't want to retrace if we can avoid it), the right formulation is: leave k-2*m_retrace nodes as walk endpoints, where m_retrace is the number of pairs we retrace. We minimise total retrace length using min-weight perfect matching on K_T, then KEEP as walk endpoints those odd nodes that would have been matched to a cost higher than 'just end the walk here'. In practice for small T (<=8 in every Latin glyph I can think of) we enumerate all pairings — networkx min_weight_matching is fine.
core_steps.pseudocode:
def decompose_component(Gc):
    odd = [n for n,d in Gc.degree() if d % 2 == 1]
    if not odd:
        # Eulerian circuit: every node even -> one closed walk.
        circuit = hierholzer_circuit(Gc, start=lowest_topmost_node(Gc))
        walks = split_circuit_at_sharp_turns(circuit, Gc)
        return walks
    if len(odd) == 2:
        u, v = odd
        path = hierholzer_trail(Gc, start=u, end=v)
        return split_trail_at_sharp_turns(path, Gc)
    # k >= 4 odd nodes. Build a weighted complete graph on odd nodes;
    # edge weight = shortest-path length in Gc between them.
    K = nx.Graph()
    for a, b in itertools.combinations(odd, 2):
        K.add_edge(a, b, weight=nx.shortest_path_length(Gc, a, b, weight='length'))
    # Min-weight perfect matching pairs every odd node. Each pair gets bridged
    # by duplicating the shortest path between them (retracing those edges).
    matching = nx.min_weight_matching(K)
    Gaug = Gc.copy()
    for a, b in matching:
        sp = nx.shortest_path(Gc, a, b, weight='length')
        for i in range(len(sp)-1):
            # duplicate the cheapest parallel edge between sp[i], sp[i+1]
            best_k = min(Gc[sp[i]][sp[i+1]], key=lambda k: Gc[sp[i]][sp[i+1]][k]['length'])
            d = Gc[sp[i]][sp[i+1]][best_k]
            Gaug.add_edge(sp[i], sp[i+1], path=d['path'], length=d['length'],
                          tan_u=d['tan_u'], tan_v=d['tan_v'], retrace=True)
    # Now Gaug is Eulerian. Read out one circuit.
    circuit = hierholzer_circuit(Gaug, start=lowest_topmost_node(Gaug))
    walks = split_circuit_at_sharp_turns(circuit, Gaug)
    # Optional: re-open the circuit at the longest retrace edge so we trade
    # one retrace for an open trail (handwriting prefers open over closed).
    return walks
core_steps.edge_cases: Self-loops contribute 2 to degree, so a single 'o' has all-even degrees and one Eulerian circuit. If matching picks pairs that are degenerate (a == b, only possible if same node appears as odd in multigraph weirdness) skip them. min_weight_matching on |T|<=10 is fast enough; we never see |T|>10 in normal Latin glyphs.

core_steps.name: Hierholzer for the Eulerian trail/circuit
core_steps.rationale: Standard. The wrinkle is: at each visit to a multi-edge junction we want to pick the *outgoing* edge whose tangent best continues the *incoming* edge's tangent. That's the single most important hand-writing-like choice — it's what makes 'M' get traced /\/\ in one motion instead of zig-zagging.
core_steps.pseudocode:
def hierholzer_trail(G, start, end=None):
    # G is a MultiGraph. We mark edges used via a set of (u,v,k).
    used = set()
    stack = [start]
    trail = []
    # incoming tangent at the current node, for continuity scoring
    in_tan = None
    while stack:
        v = stack[-1]
        # candidate edges out of v
        cands = [(u, w, k) for u, w, k in G.edges(v, keys=True)
                 if (u, w, k) not in used and (w, u, k) not in used]
        if not cands:
            trail.append(stack.pop())
            continue
        # Score each candidate by tangent continuity with in_tan.
        # Lower is better (smaller turning angle). Ties broken by:
        # prefer non-retrace, then prefer longer edge (stay on main stroke).
        def score(c):
            u, w, k = c
            d = G[u][w][k]
            t_out = d['tan_u'] if u == v else d['tan_v']
            if in_tan is None:
                return (0,)                                # no preference
            ang = angle_between(in_tan, -np.array(t_out))  # turning angle
            return (ang, d.get('retrace', False), -d['length'])
        u, w, k = min(cands, key=score)
        used.add((u, w, k))
        nxt = w if u == v else u
        d = G[u][w][k]
        in_tan = d['tan_v'] if u == v else d['tan_u']      # tangent leaving nxt-side
        stack.append(nxt)
    trail.reverse()
    return trail   # list of skeleton-graph nodes; reconstruct pixels below
core_steps.edge_cases: Self-loops: a self-loop edge (u,u,k) must be picked exactly like any other edge from u; its 'tan_u' and 'tan_v' are different vectors (both leaving u, in opposite ends of the loop). When we choose it we mark used and stay at u. Disconnected after edge removal — Hierholzer's nested-stack form handles this naturally as long as the graph is Eulerian to begin with. If start has odd degree we need start to be one of the odd endpoints; for circuit form we require all-even and pick the leftmost-topmost node.

core_steps.name: Split the long trail at sharp tangent reversals
core_steps.rationale: Even after the continuity-scoring during Hierholzer, the trail may pass through a junction where the LEAST-bad next edge still requires a >110° turn. That's a place a human picks up the pen. This is the single post-processing step that converts one Eulerian trail into the natural stroke count (e.g. 'A' -> 3, 'M' -> 1 or 2 depending on style, 't' -> 2).
core_steps.pseudocode:
SHARP_TURN = math.radians(110)

def split_trail_at_sharp_turns(node_trail, G):
    # Reconstruct pixel-level polylines, splitting wherever the turn
    # at a junction exceeds SHARP_TURN.
    walks = []
    current = []
    for i, n in enumerate(node_trail):
        if i == 0:
            current = [n]
            continue
        u, v = node_trail[i-1], n
        # pick the unused edge that we walked (Hierholzer order guarantees one)
        k = pop_walked_edge(G, u, v)
        d = G[u][v][k]
        pix = d['path'] if d['path'][0] == u else d['path'][::-1]
        current.append(pix)
        # Check turn at the junction we just LEFT (node u, if i>=2)
        if i >= 2 and G.degree(u) >= 3:
            t_in  = tangent_into(node_trail[i-2], u, G)    # tangent arriving at u
            t_out = tangent_out_of(u, v, G)                # tangent leaving u
            turn = math.pi - angle_between(t_in, t_out)    # 0=straight, pi=reversal
            if turn > SHARP_TURN:
                # split BEFORE this edge — close current walk up to u,
                # start a new walk from u with the new edge.
                walks.append(concat_pixels(current[:-1]))
                current = [u, pix]
    walks.append(concat_pixels(current))
    return [w for w in walks if len(w) >= 2]

# For closed circuits, we rotate the circuit so the rotation start is the
# sharpest turn — that way the circuit gets cut at the most pen-up-natural
# spot and possibly degenerates into a single walk that starts where a
# human would start (e.g. top of 'o').
def split_circuit_at_sharp_turns(node_circuit, G):
    turns = compute_turn_at_each_position(node_circuit, G)
    cut = argmax(turns)
    if turns[cut] < SHARP_TURN:
        # smoothly closed loop: cut at top-most point for handwriting feel
        cut = top_most_position(node_circuit)
    rotated = node_circuit[cut:] + node_circuit[1:cut+1]
    return split_trail_at_sharp_turns(rotated, G)
core_steps.edge_cases: Two consecutive sharp turns at the same junction (rare but possible at the apex of 'M' if both /\ legs meet at >55° each) — both splits fire and we get the natural three-stroke decomposition. For self-loops the 'turn at u' check is degenerate because u == v at both ends; treat the self-loop's two tangents as the in/out tangents directly. SHARP_TURN=110° is a tunable; lower values produce more strokes (cleaner per-stroke but less natural), higher produces fewer (more retrace, less natural).

core_steps.name: Order walks for handwriting and pick start points
core_steps.rationale: For each walk, pick the endpoint to start at that a human would: top before bottom, left before right, with two exceptions — capital letters that start with a downstroke from the top-left (A, B, M, N, …) and lowercase letters with a leading down-stroke. The simple rule 'start at the topmost endpoint, break ties leftmost' covers ~all of Latin a–z A–Z correctly.
core_steps.pseudocode:
def order_walks_for_handwriting(walks):
    # Sort walks: components top-to-bottom by their topmost pixel,
    # then left-to-right by leftmost pixel.
    walks_oriented = []
    for w in walks:
        # endpoints of the polyline (first and last point)
        a, b = w[0], w[-1]
        # if it's a closed walk, find the topmost pixel and rotate there
        if a == b and len(w) > 2:
            top_idx = min(range(len(w)), key=lambda i: (w[i][0], w[i][1]))
            w = w[top_idx:] + w[1:top_idx+1]
            walks_oriented.append(w)
            continue
        # open walk: orient so we start at the topmost endpoint
        if (b[0], b[1]) < (a[0], a[1]):
            w = w[::-1]
        walks_oriented.append(w)
    walks_oriented.sort(key=lambda w: (w[0][0], w[0][1]))
    return walks_oriented
core_steps.edge_cases: Floating-dot components ('i', 'j', '?', '!') sort to last because they have a higher top-y than the stem. Wait — in image coordinates the dot has a SMALLER y (it's higher up). Good: that means the dot sorts first under (y, x). That's wrong for handwriting (you write the stem first, then the dot). So: special-case — if a component's bounding box is tiny (< 0.3 * mean component size), push it to the end of the order. That's the entire 'i/j/!/?' fix.

handles_letters.notes: G_skel has one node (the loop's self-loop endpoint introduced by skeleton_to_graph) or zero nodes with a single closed cycle. All degrees even (the self-loop contributes 2). Hierholzer produces one circuit; no sharp turns -> not split. Rotated to start at topmost pixel. Result: 1 walk starting at 12 o'clock going counterclockwise (which is what 'a' or 'o' first stroke looks like).
Two endpoints (degrees 1 and 1, both odd). |T|=2, no matching needed; one trail from top to bottom. No junctions, no splits. Topmost endpoint becomes start. Result: 1 walk.

handles_letters.topology_class: tree-with-1-junction (4 endpoints + 1 crossbar) — actually two junctions: left-leg/crossbar and right-leg/crossbar
handles_letters.notes: Skeleton: two junctions J_L, J_R where crossbar meets legs; endpoints E_top (apex, but apex is itself a junction if pruning leaves a small triangle — usually it's one apex junction A_top + two foot endpoints E_LF, E_RF + crossbar endpoints absorbed into J_L,J_R). After junction-merging A_top may be a single apex node of degree 2 or 3. Take the typical case: apex degree 2 (apex absorbs both legs' top), two leg-bottom endpoints E_LF, E_RF, and crossbar runs J_L-J_R. Odd-degree count: E_LF (1), E_RF (1), J_L (3), J_R (3). |T|=4. min-weight matching pairs (E_LF↔J_L, E_RF↔J_R) at cost = short stub-up-the-leg. Better: matching pairs (J_L↔J_R) via the crossbar (already 1 edge so 'retrace' cost = crossbar length) and (E_LF↔E_RF) via both legs (cost = full perimeter). The matching solver picks the cheaper: (E_LF↔J_L) + (E_RF↔J_R), meaning we retrace the tiny stubs of leg-below-crossbar. Hierholzer with continuity scoring then traces /\\ + crossbar + retrace. Sharp-turn splitting at J_L (we arrive going down-left from apex, leave going right along crossbar — turn ~120°) splits there; similarly at J_R. Result: 3 walks — left leg (apex -> E_LF), right leg (apex -> E_RF), crossbar (J_L -> J_R). Note: the apex starts both leg walks because tangent continuity says the smoothest pen-up is at the apex itself. The pipeline emits two walks both starting at the apex, which matches how a human writes A.

handles_letters.topology_class: tree with 0 internal junctions (5 endpoints if apex is sharp, 3 endpoints + 2 junctions if /\/\ shape merges at valleys/peaks)
handles_letters.notes: Typical sans-serif M: 4 endpoints (bottom-left, bottom-right, valley-bottom is NOT an endpoint, two top peaks are NOT endpoints — actually depends on the font). A common skeleton: 2 bottom endpoints + 1 valley junction (degree 3 where two inner diagonals meet at the bottom-middle) + 2 top peaks (degree 2 absorbed). Then odd nodes are just the 2 bottom endpoints; |T|=2, one trail. Continuity scoring at the valley junction will pick the through-route (up the right diagonal after coming down the left, NOT a U-turn back up the same leg). Sharp-turn splitting: at the valley the turn is ~120° (down-then-up), so we split — result: 2 walks (/\ left half, /\ right half). For a serif M with vertical outer legs we get 4 walks (left stem, left diagonal, right diagonal, right stem).
