Honest: this is sensitive to the SHARP_TURN threshold and to whether the valley is one junction or two.

handles_letters.topology_class: tree with 2 junctions (3 stems hanging off a top arch)
handles_letters.notes: Skeleton: 3 bottom endpoints E1, E2, E3; 2 junctions J1 (top of stem 1 meets top arch), J2 (top of stem 2 meets top arch); E_top maybe absorbed. Degrees: E1=1, E2=1, E3=1, J1=3, J2=3, top-left endpoint=1. So odd nodes: 4 endpoints + 2 junctions = 6. |T|=6 -> matching pairs three. Min-weight matching picks the cheapest 3 pairs; for a balanced 'm' these are (E1↔J1), (E2↔J2)... wait, E2 is the middle stem bottom. The cheapest matching pairs the junctions with the nearest endpoints, meaning we retrace the short top-of-stem segments. Hierholzer then produces walks following the natural arch-up-arch-up motion. Sharp-turn splitting at J1, J2 (arriving going up the stem, leaving going right along the arch — 90° turn) cuts there. Result: typically 1 walk if SHARP_TURN=110° (90° doesn't split) — which is correct for cursive m. For print m we'd want 3 strokes (stem | arch+stem | arch+stem); lowering SHARP_TURN to 80° produces that. Honest: this is the letter where the threshold matters most.

handles_letters.topology_class: stem with closed bowl (one junction degree 3)
handles_letters.notes: Skeleton: top-of-stem endpoint E_top, bowl-junction J where stem meets bowl (degree 3: up, down to bowl-start, into-bowl-end). Wait — bowl is a closed loop; after collapse_parallel_edges and the loop's natural self-closure, the bowl appears as a self-loop on J. Then degrees: E_top=1, J=1+2(self-loop)=3, bottom-of-stem if separate=1. Most fonts: stem extends below the bowl too OR ends at the bowl. Assume it ends at the bowl: E_top=1 (odd), J=3 (odd). |T|=2. One trail from E_top to J: down the stem, then once around the bowl, ending at J. Sharp-turn check at J on the second pass: arriving from stem going down, leaving into bowl going right — turn ~90°, no split. After bowl, arriving at J going up, ending — no further step. Result: 1 walk. Hmm, expected 2: humans write b as stem-down then bowl. Fix: the cycle-vs-stem split should be a separate sharp-turn check because the turn at J going from stem-into-bowl is exactly 90° which is borderline. With SHARP_TURN=85° this splits into [stem-down, bowl-around] = 2 walks. Honest: this is fragile; a more principled rule is 'if a self-loop hangs off a degree-3 node, always split the loop into its own walk'. Easy to add.

handles_letters.topology_class: stem with two closed bowls (two junctions or one middle junction with two self-loops)
handles_letters.notes: Two cases depending on font. Cursive B: middle junction J_mid (degree 4: two stem segments + two bowl entries), each bowl is a self-loop. Degrees: E_top=1, E_bot=1, J_mid=2+2+2=6. |T|=2. One trail E_top -> stem-down -> J_mid -> upper-bowl-around -> J_mid -> lower-bowl-around -> J_mid -> stem-down -> E_bot. The two bowls and the stem get split by sharp-turn rule + 'self-loop hangs off junction' rule into 3 walks. Honest: again threshold-dependent; the 'self-loop = own walk' rule cleanly produces 3 walks (stem, upper bowl, lower bowl), which matches how I write B.

Skeleton: E_top (stem top), E_bot (stem bottom), E_left (crossbar left), E_right (crossbar right), J (stem-crossbar intersection, degree 4). Degrees: E_top=1, E_bot=1, E_left=1, E_right=1, J=4. |T|=4, all four endpoints are odd. Min-weight matching: cheapest pairing is (E_top↔E_bot) via stem (long but unavoidable) + (E_left↔E_right) via crossbar (long but unavoidable). That gives zero retrace! Trail: enter at E_top -> down stem -> J -> across crossbar (continuity at J picks the perpendicular continuation? NO — continuity picks straight-through, but stem is vertical and crossbar is horizontal, so 'continuation' is a 90° turn either way. Hierholzer's tangent score is INDIFFERENT among the three remaining edges at J). Whichever is picked, sharp-turn splitting at J (arriving down, leaving horizontal: 90° -> splits at SHARP_TURN=85°). Result: 2 walks — vertical stem (E_top to E_bot), horizontal crossbar (E_left to E_right). Matches handwriting. Honest: with SHARP_TURN=110° this would NOT split and we'd get one zig-zag walk — wrong. SHARP_TURN must be ≤90° to handle t (and +) correctly. Recommended default: 85°.

handles_letters.topology_class: stem with two diagonals (one junction degree 4)
handles_letters.notes: Skeleton: E_stem_top, E_stem_bot, E_diag_up_right, E_diag_down_right, J (stem-diagonal meeting point, degree 4 if both diagonals meet at one point; degree 3+3 if they meet at slightly different points which is more typical). Take degree-4 case: |T|=4 (all four endpoints odd), matching pairs (stem_top↔stem_bot) + (diag_up↔diag_down). Trail = stem-down then enter J, go up-right (or down-right), reach endpoint, no more edges at that endpoint -> backtrack? No, Hierholzer doesn't backtrack — it would use min-weight matching to retrace. Actually with the matching above, the augmented graph adds a duplicate stem edge AND a duplicate diagonal edge through J, making J degree 8 (even). pitfalls: Honest self-critique: (1) SHARP_TURN threshold is a single global constant doing too much work. 't' wants ≤90°, 'm' wants ≥100°, 'b' wants the borderline-90° case to split. There's no single value that handles every letter perfectly across every font. A real implementation should make this per-junction-aware: if the junction is at a stroke endpoint (degree 3 with one short stub), use a low threshold; if it's a smooth tangent merge (degree 3 with all three edges meeting at near-equal angles), use a high one. Adds ~30 lines and I haven't proved it converges on the full Latin set. (2) min-weight matching minimises retrace LENGTH but handwriting cares about retrace VISIBILITY and stroke-count too. For 'k', pure min-weight matching can produce a four-walk decomposition where two walks both pass through the same junction in a way that looks like scribbling. The fix (prefer matchings that touch fewer odd nodes shared) is a real wart. (3) The 'self-loop = its own walk' rule for 'b', 'B', 'p', 'q' isn't elegant — it's a special case grafted on. A more principled formulation: after the Eulerian decomposition, run a SECOND pass that looks at each walk and asks 'does this walk traverse a closed sub-walk that starts and ends at the same node?'. If yes, optionally cut. But that doubles the post-processing complexity. (4) The Hierholzer continuity scoring is greedy. At a degree-4 junction with three remaining unused edges, picking the locally-best continuation can leave a worse continuation for later. A globally-optimal version would be an exponential-time search; in practice the greedy version is fine because junctions are small. (5) Closed components (Eulerian circuits without any odd nodes — 'o', 'O', possibly the bowl of 'a' if treated as one component) get their start point chosen by topmost-pixel, which produces counterclockwise traces for 'o'. Real handwriting goes clockwise for 'o'. Easy fix: flip orientation if the signed area of the closed walk is positive (we'd be going CCW in image coordinates). One extra line, but I haven't put it in the pseudocode. (6) The whole approach assumes the skeleton + junction merging is correct. If `merge_nearby_junctions` leaves two unmerged degree-3 nodes 25px apart at what should be one 'X' crossing, the matching and Hierholzer still work but produce two near-coincident strokes — visually wrong. The current 22px threshold is OK for 384-512px renders but couples our algorithm to the existing preprocessing. (7) Line count check: build_skel_graph reuses existing code (0 new lines).
